about.title: Turlock Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall rarely gives you warning. One moment you are stepping out of a store along Geer Road or crossing a parking lot off W Main Street in downtown Turlock, and the next you are on the ground trying to piece together what happened. California premises liability law puts responsibility on the owner or the business in control of a space when they knew about a hazard, or reasonably should have known, and neither fixed it nor warned people. That 'notice' element is where these claims are won or lost, so what you gather in the first few days carries real weight: photos of the spill, the broken step, or the unmarked drop-off; names of anyone who saw you fall; and a prompt written request that the business keep its surveillance footage before it is recorded over. Turlock is a Stanislaus County city of roughly 72,000 people, and the attorneys LawProactive connects you with understand how claims here move. Our service is free, and every network attorney works on contingency.

whyChoose.title: Why Turlock Residents Turn to LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Attorneys Who Know How to Prove Notice
items.desc: Showing that an owner knew or should have known about a hazard takes more than your word. The attorneys in our network dig into maintenance logs, inspection schedules, prior complaints, and video to build that piece of the case.

items.title: Deadlines Handled Before They Become Problems
items.desc: California gives you two years to file most premises liability lawsuits, but a fall on city, county, or other public property triggers a much shorter government claim window. Getting connected early keeps those dates from slipping past.

items.title: Fair Treatment Under Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if an insurer argues you were partly to blame, you can still recover a share reduced by your percentage. An independent attorney can push back when that percentage is inflated.

items.question: I tripped on a broken sidewalk in Turlock. Is the city responsible?
items.answer: It depends on who owns and controls that stretch of pavement, which in Turlock could be the City, Stanislaus County, or an adjacent property owner. If a public entity is involved, California requires you to file an administrative claim within a much shorter window than the usual two-year deadline, generally six months. Photograph the exact spot, note the nearest cross street such as Lander Avenue or N Golden State Boulevard, and get connected with an attorney quickly so the right claim goes to the right agency in time.

items.question: The store says there is no camera footage. What can I do?
items.answer: Many businesses do have cameras, and footage is often overwritten within days or weeks. An attorney can send a formal preservation letter right away, which puts the business on notice that deleting the video could hurt their position later. Even without footage, incident reports, witness statements, and your own photos can still establish that the hazard existed and how long it had been there.

items.question: I was looking at my phone when I fell. Do I still have a claim?
items.answer: Possibly, yes. California's pure comparative fault rule means being partly at fault does not bar recovery; it reduces it by your share of the blame. The core question remains whether the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to address it. An attorney from our network can look at the facts honestly and tell you where you stand.
